# Introduction {#sec-intro -}

<!-- RAP (2026-10-13, Hans): measurement and cost (detect, measure, fiscal cost + cost to productivity measurement); review: Thesis/feedback/jmp-abstract-rap-131026.md. Earlier options (RAP 2, tax rates, chosen 2026-09-24): Thesis/feedback/jmp-intro-rap-options.md -->

<!-- Firms owned by the highest earners evade more tax through cost overreporting than firms owned by lower-income earners: relative to the bottom 80 percent of the income distribution, the tax evaded in Ecuador by the top 5 percent, as a share of owners' income, is 56 times larger [@Carrillo2022]. -->

Tax evasion through overreporting of input costs arises when firms inflate their reported purchases to claim additional deductions against their value-added tax (VAT) liabilities. Despite its relevance, we still do not know much about firms' cost overreporting. Tax authorities around the world document that this kind of evasion, often through fictitious invoices, is costly and widespread [@OECD2017]. The losses amount to between 1.2 and 2.7 percent of total tax revenue in Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Poland, and Slovakia, and about a ninth of the entire VAT compliance gap in Colombia and Slovakia [@OECD2017; @Carrillo2022; @CASE2018; @Pelaez2022]. Because some of these figures are tax administrations' own estimates, and all are conditional on detected evasion, true losses are plausibly larger.

Measuring firms' cost overreporting has been limited to studies based on tax records [@Carrillo2022; @Zumaya2021]. These studies with transaction-level tax records in Ecuador and Mexico show that firms acquire fake invoices to overreport costs [@Carrillo2022; @Zumaya2021]. Tax records, however, are confidential, available for few countries, and accessible only to selected researchers. Without them, economists infer evasion from validation samples, comparing an indirect measure of true income between a truth-reporting group and a group that may misreport [@Pissarides1989; @Gorodnichenko2009]. This approach however was built for individuals. For firms, the natural indirect measure, output relative to inputs, also depends on an additional unobservable, productivity: a firm reporting high input use, for a given level of output, may be either overreporting or simply less productive.

I ask whether input overreporting can be detected and measured from standard production data, and how large are its costs. I study these questions with a Colombian manufacturing survey from 1981 to 1991. During this period, the Colombian sales tax worked as a VAT, and the data include a subset of firms that, due to government and market scrutiny, reported inputs correctly. I find that overreporting can be detected and measured from these data alone, that it is common and large, and that it is costly in two ways: for the government, which credits fictitious purchases, and for productivity measurement, in particular for proxy-variable methods that rely on the flexible input, the one firms overreport, materials.

To distinguish between overreporting and productivity, I use a structural production-function approach and a benchmark group of firms that report inputs correctly. In the absence of evasion, the first-order condition for materials shows that the firm's materials share of revenue is equal to the common technology in an industry. Government and market scrutiny keep corporations from overreporting. Corporations are thus the benchmark that identifies the common technology in each industry and the distribution of measurement error in output. Among unincorporated firms, deviations from the common technology reveal overreporting up to measurement error in output. Deconvolution allows for separating the distribution of overreporting from that of the measurement error. Finally, employing an entropy-based method [@Schennach2014], I estimate a structural model in which firms choose inputs and overreporting to maximize expected after-tax profits. In the model, firms choose the tax evaded weighing the probability of detection and a cost of evasion that varies with productivity.

Overreporting can be detected with a simple and robust statistical test. Under the null hypothesis of correct reporting, the test is agnostic about the specification of both the probability of detection and the cost of overreporting, and its size holds under any common production technology. A rejection is also unambiguous becuase no firm gains by underreporting deductible inputs. Among the 20 largest industries, the test detects overreporting in 9 of the 18 industries liable for the sales tax, which together produce about two fifths of manufacturing output, including 4 of the 5 largest. It detects no overreporting in either of the 2 food industries, which were exempt from the sales tax.

Overreporting is large and responds to the tax rate that rewards it. By deconvolution, I recover the distribution of overreporting in each industry. In the five largest industries where the test rejects at the 1 percent level and the deconvolution applies, unincorporated firms overreport on average between 4.5 and 23.1 percent of their true materials, depending on the industry. Overreporting also rose with the tax rate. Between 1983 and 1987, after Colombia raised the sales-tax rate for most manufacturing industries, overreporting by unincorporated firms in the affected industries rose significantly, by about 8.5 percentage points of true materials. The response implies a midpoint elasticity of overreporting with respect to the tax rate of 5.9.

Overreporting is costly for the government. In the structural model, undetected overreporting costs 4.7 percent of the gross sales-tax revenue from unincorporated firms in the industries where overreporting is detected. A 1 percent increase in the rate on purchases lowers net sales-tax revenue by about 1.7 percent of gross sales-tax revenue. Because net sales-tax revenue is negative at the observed rate (the sales-tax refunds on claimed deductions exceed the gross sales-tax revenue from sales), a cut of about 17 percent in the rate on purchases would make it break even, and a cut of about 28 percent or more would make it significantly positive, at the 5 percent level.

Overreporting is also costly for productivity measurement. Proxy-variable methods that rely on a flexible input typically define it as materials [@Levinsohn2003; @Doraszelski2013; @Ackerberg2015; @Gandhi2020]. But this is the input firms overreport. In the five industries of the deconvolution, the uncorrected estimates show output elasticities of materials that are consistently larger, and productivity distributions that are more dispersed and less persistent, than the corrected ones. In the median of the five industries, the ratio of the 90th to the 10th percentile is 66 percent larger and the half-life of productivity shocks is 63 percent shorter.

## Relation to the literature {-}

These results relate to three strands of public economics and to one of productivity measurement. First, I provide measures of firms' cost overreporting without relying on confidential tax records. Most evidence on firm evasion focuses on underreported revenue [@Slemrod2019], yet the cost side matters. Firms offset enforcement on revenue by raising reported costs [@Carrillo2017; @Asatryan2017], and paper trails make transactions between firms harder to misreport than sales to final consumers [@Pomeranz2015]; therefore, firms that sell to other firms have little room to misreport on the sales side and more on the cost side. Survey-based measures of firm evasion rely on firms' self-reported share of sales declared to the tax authority [@Dabla2019], whose truthfulness cannot be verified. My approach needs only reported inputs and output, and is thus equally applicable to standard firm-level surveys, administrative records, and confidential tax records.

Second, I extend the validation-sample approach from individuals to firms. In its classic application, the self-employed report less income relative to their food consumption than employees, whose income is reported by their employers [@Pissarides1989], and the same comparison has measured how evasion responds to a tax reform [@Gorodnichenko2009]. I use the production function to separate overreporting from productivity, with corporations as the truth-reporting group. Unlike the comparisons for individuals, my approach does not require the two groups to be alike in size or productivity: corporations are much larger than unincorporated firms, and the production function accounts for the differences in productivity behind this gap.

Third, [the paper]{.content-visible when-meta="jmp"}[this thesis]{.content-hidden when-meta="jmp"} shows how tax-motivated overreporting of inputs biases production-function estimates. Proxy-variable methods rely on a flexible input, typically materials, either inverting its demand [@Levinsohn2003; @Ackerberg2015] or using its first-order condition [@Gandhi2020]. These methods treat reported inputs as true. Work on mismeasured inputs has focused on classical measurement error (mean zero and independent of the true input), mostly in capital [@Collard2020]. Overreporting is neither: firms choose it based on their own productivity. Furthermore, it affects exactly the input on which these methods rely. Correcting for it matters for any analysis built on measured productivity differences across firms.

Finally, I estimate how a particular form of evasion by firms responds to the tax rate, a response that the literature on taxes and revenue has mostly studied through individuals' reported income. Traditionally, the elasticity of personal taxable income has combined all the different responses to the rate, evasion included, into a single statistic [@Feldstein1999; @SlemrodKopczuk2002; @Saez2012]. However, when part of the cost of evasion is a transfer rather than a resource cost, this elasticity alone no longer measures the efficiency cost of taxation [@Chetty2009]. Measuring that cost requires knowing how evasion itself responds to the rate, separately from real activity. Direct evidence on this response is scarcer, and comes from the gap between households' consumption and reported income [@Gorodnichenko2009] and, for firms, from bunching at kinks and notches in the tax schedule [@Best2015; @Almunia2018]. I provide evidence for firms' overreporting of inputs under a sales tax that credits purchases, from both a statutory rate change and a structural model that separates overreporting from productivity. The structural model also speaks to the theory of optimal commodity taxation under evasion by estimating how claimed deductions respond to the rate [@Cremer1993].

The rest of the paper follows the argument. @sec-setting describes the Colombian sales tax, which credited purchases, and explains why Colombian corporations can serve as truth-tellers. @sec-model shows how the tax rate generates incentives for a firm to overreport materials, and how its optimal choice depends on the probability of detection and the cost of evasion. @sec-testing shows how overreporting can be detected and measured from production data alone. Then, @sec-pf demonstrates how failing to correct for overreporting biases production-function and productivity estimates. @sec-fiscal leverages the 1983 reform to document that overreporting responds to the tax rate. @sec-counterfactual estimates the firm's evasion decision and the cost of undetected overreporting, and shows that a 1 percent increase in the rate on purchases lowers net sales-tax revenue by about 1.7 percent of gross sales-tax revenue. @sec-conclusion, as tradition demands, concludes.

::: {.content-hidden when-meta="jmp"}
The rest of the thesis follows the argument. @sec-model shows why a firm would overreport materials and what holds it back, and @sec-setting explains why Colombian corporations can serve as truth-tellers. @sec-testing shows that overreporting can be detected from production data alone, @sec-deconvolution measures how much firms overreport, and @sec-pf shows what correcting for it does to production-function estimates. @sec-fiscal uses the 1983 reform to show that overreporting responds to the tax rate, and @sec-counterfactual asks how much claimed deductions would move under other rates. @sec-literature relates these results to the literature, and @sec-conclusion, as tradition demands, concludes.
